claims.text: Sufficient thermomechanical energy induces local compositional segregation at high-strain dislocation interfaces in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Local segregation promotes nucleation of nanoscale brittle intermetallic or solute-rich precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates act as preferred crack-initiation sites and degrade toughness.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase compositionally complex alloy without pre-existing brittle precipitates.
Elevated-temperature cycling or slow-strain-rate deformation at high plastic strain promotes thermally assisted diffusion and local segregation.
Sustained stress and moderate thermal activation can permit local diffusion without causing bulk-scale phase separation.

Compositional segregation, including formation of Cu-rich and other solute-enriched regions, can coexist with nanoscale phase interfaces and dislocation-wall boundaries in a deformed high-entropy alloy.
The solute-enriched regions formed at strain-induced interfaces are brittle nanoscale precipitates.
Dislocation activity creates highly distorted regions that act as sinks for solute atoms.
Local compositional fluctuations drive spinodal-like decomposition or precipitation at the nanoscale.
The precipitates concentrate along deformation paths and act as stress concentrators.
Precipitate stress concentration lowers the energy required for crack initiation and propagation.
Thermomechanically loaded samples will develop localized nanoscale precipitates at dislocation interfaces relative to the homogeneous baseline.
Thermomechanically loaded samples will exhibit increased local hardness.
Thermomechanically loaded samples will exhibit a measurable reduction in fracture toughness.
The onset of brittle failure will correlate with precipitate density and size.
The homogeneous as-cast or minimally deformed baseline exhibits high toughness and ductility.
Extremely low temperature or very rapid deformation suppresses the proposed brittle behavior by limiting diffusion and segregation time.
The strain, temperature, dwell-time, and elemental thresholds for initiating significant segregation are not established.
Failure to observe both localized brittle precipitates and a toughness reduction under segregation-promoting conditions would refute the proposed mechanism.
